stances.claim: Sean Borja's essay (selected as the column's featured sample) demonstrates that the liberty-and-prosperity philosophy can be grounded in concrete narratives -- moving from constitutional abstraction (Art II Sec 9) through SC social-justice jurisprudence to a 9-year-old street vendor's daily reality, modeling the very advocacy-to-the-underserved bridge that the FLP scholarship requires.
stances.rhetorical_move: exemplar-selection framing (one scholar's essay as proof-of-concept for the scholarship's philosophical formation)

stances.claim: Justice is not merely about giving -- it must be ENABLING; the SC's own jurisprudence rejects 'division of property or equality of economic status' in favor of equality of opportunity, political rights, legal protection, value-exchange equity, and effort-based sharing of social/material goods -- making prosperity and liberty inseparable: 'One without the other would simply not do.'
stances.rhetorical_move: definitional-clarification + binary-inseparability argument (justice ≠ giving but enabling; prosperity ⇔ liberty)
stances.confidence: asserted via Borja's voice quoting SC jurisprudence

stances.claim: Lander Solano's narrative is one of myriad stories needing to be heard -- and a constitutional discussion of Article II is 'a highfalutin', largely academic exercise unless it can be concretized and brought down to the level of the common tao'; the lawyer's task is to stand at the helm of the law and through advocacy 'turn liberty and prosperity into concrete reality.'
stances.rhetorical_move: abstract-to-concrete bridge (Constitution → kesong puti vendor) + lawyer-as-bridging-instrument argument

stances.claim: Without lawyers as bridging agency, the rule of law is rendered 'fictional and out of reach' for those at society's fringes -- making the lawyer's mission to learn advocacy and 'become the voice that resonates when others go silent' a structural necessity, not optional vocation.
stances.rhetorical_move: rule-of-law dependency on lawyer-agency for the underserved

notable_anecdotes: Lander 'Little Prince' Solano -- 9 years old, selling kesong puti along Filmore Street in Makati, 'in the company of thieves' through alleys, flyovers, and underpasses -- currently out of school but aspiring to engineering to 'build homes, towers, and dreams'; the most viscerally specific narrative anchor in any FLP-related column.

Lander's mother vending kesong puti behind Cash & Carry along Osmeña Highway and the family sleeping there when goods remain unsold -- adding intergenerational poverty texture to the single-child portrait.

Borja's opening register: 'In the age of millennials, where choice is virtually unlimited, choosing a career path is a quarterlife crisis waiting to happen. Luckily for me, that was not the case' -- the column's only direct concession to the millennial generational frame.

Borja's coined-phrase ending: 'become the voice that resonates when others go silent' -- the column's title 'Resonance' draws from this single phrase, making the title itself a citation of the scholar's voice.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban features the essay of 1st-batch FLP LibPros scholar Sean Borja (Ateneo de Manila) -- abstracted in Borja's own words -- as the column's centerpiece. Borja begins with his vocational certainty since high school's junior year -- sparing him the millennial 'quarterlife crisis' -- but acknowledging that wanting to be a lawyer did not equal understanding what lawyers do. He grounds the answer in Article II Section 9 of the Constitution, which commands the state to 'promote a just and dynamic social order' ensuring prosperity, independence, and freedom from poverty -- making 'Prosperity for all' the goal of social justice. He cites SC jurisprudence: social justice does not champion division of property or equality of economic status but rather 'equality of opportunity, equality of political rights, equality before the law, equality between values given and received, and equitable sharing of the social and material goods on the basis of efforts exerted in their production' -- concluding that justice must be ENABLING, not merely benevolent, and that 'One without the other would simply not do.' He grounds the abstraction in the story of 'Little Prince' Lander Solano, a 9-year-old kesong puti vendor on Filmore Street in Makati who navigates alleys, flyovers, and underpasses daily 'in the company of thieves,' currently out of school but aspiring to engineering; his mother also vends kesong puti behind the Cash & Carry on Osmeña Highway where the family sleeps when goods remain unsold. Borja closes that the rule of law is 'the great equalizer' but 'without lawyers, the law is rendered fictional and out of reach, especially for those at the fringes of society' -- making the lawyer's mission to learn advocacy and 'become the voice that resonates when others go silent,' which gives the column its title.
